title.zh: 伦敦迷幻和地下迷幻文化

summary.en: While San Francisco psychedelia was in full swing, London across the water developed a psychedelic culture with a subtle relationship to it.
summary.zh: 在旧金山迷幻如火如荼之时，隔岸相望的伦敦发展出了与其关系微妙的迷幻文化体系

body.zh:
在旧金山迷幻如火如荼之时，隔岸相望的伦敦发展出了与其关系微妙的迷幻文化体系

现在让我们穿过美洲大陆，跨越大西洋，从旧金山来到伦敦，来讲讲这里迷幻文化的发展情况，以及一些英美迷幻异同比较的讨论。

在1967年前的第一阶段，我们能在伦敦找到些与旧金山一致的东西——我们所熟知的那些主流乐队割据榜单，不过后来他们也和伦敦的亚文化交织在了一起。伦敦的迷幻亚文化在1965年业已出现，和旧金山的情况相同，1967年有几只迷幻乐队崛起，迷幻文化突然风靡全国。其中有些乐队在美国取得了成功，有些则没有。英国迷幻文化发展中有一个有趣的现象，那就是在英国发展迷幻音乐的那些人实际上对于旧金山的情况所知甚少——毕竟1965、1966年乘飞机还没有现在这么普遍，没多少人会在旧金山和纽约之间来来去去，特别是只有20、21岁的年轻人。因此那个时候，伦敦人了解旧金山的信息渠道其实都是道听途说，或者是报纸上报道的。而那时候针对年轻人的报纸还不是很多，就更别提电视节目了——当时还没有互联网和卫星电视，你怎么知道旧金山究竟发生了什么呢？然而有意思的是，这些年轻人在有限的信息基础上，发展出了一种在某种程度上包含了所有旧金山基本特色的，却带有英伦口音的迷幻音乐，但事实上这两个地区其实没有直接的联系。尽管确实有人会在旧金山和伦敦之间往来，但这样的人很少，其中便包括“垮掉派”诗人Allen Ginsberg。

其实，旧金山的迷幻文化与“垮掉的一代”伴随着City Lights书店和Lawrence Ferlinghetti这样的人在50年代末就已经兴起了——不过垮掉的一代选择的音乐是爵士而不是摇滚。Allen Ginsberg不仅在垮掉派诗歌的崛起中起到重要作用，还带来了这样一种想法：使用LSD是一种提高感知能力，以及带来更多写诗灵感的途径。1965年的夏天，他来到伦敦协助当地诗人组织诗歌读书会，同时也把旧金山的一些东西带到了伦敦。1965年夏天，他们在皇家阿尔伯特音乐厅举办了一场名为“Poets of the World - Poets of Our Time”的集会，学者通常把这场集会视为某种意义上的伦敦地下迷幻文化的开端。在集会中，很多去过旧金山的人分享了他们的所见所闻。在1965年的秋天，Michael Hollingshead开设了“世界迷幻中心” (World Psychedelic Center) ，那里成为了伦敦迷幻文化的中心。他的工作和旧金山的Ken Kesey相似，也像是LSD界和整个反正统文化界的Johnny Appleseed 。在某种程度上，这也是地下正在进行的事情。

继“世界迷幻中心“开张后，1966年2月Indica书店也开张了，这家书店对反主流文化书籍的传播起到了重要作用 。John Lennon也去过这家书店，买了一本Timothy Leary的《The Psychedelic Experience》——The Beatles在1966年发行的 《Tomorrow Never Knows》 某种程度上借鉴了这本书。1966年，伦敦免费学校（London Free School）创立，这所学校致力于开设免费课程来提升人们对各种社会文化的意识，还传播各种实用的文章和论题。这所学校创办的报纸《International Times》就像是伦敦版的《The Oracle》或是后来的《Rolling Stone》，这些事都发生在1966年10月。1966年12月UFO俱乐部开办，晚上这里会开展一些充满迷幻色彩的活动。

与伦敦地下文化相对的主流文化的一个重要事件是1966年4月《Time》写了一个关于“摇摆伦敦“（Swinging London) 的故事——如果你在1966年来到伦敦，你会看到一个《Austin Powers》里取笑的Mod伦敦——那个伦敦不怎么嬉皮对吧？ 那个有着 Carnaby街 （以出售时装闻名） 和Mod风格的伦敦就是那时主流文化的情况。而当《Time》杂志向想去伦敦度假的美国人宣传这些东西的时候，伦敦的迷幻文化正在他们去不到的地方慢慢发芽。伦敦迷幻最棒的一个乐队叫Pink Floyd，那时候Pink Floyd还是Syd Barrett领导下的初始阵容。他们早先的两首单曲在英国举足轻重，但是在美国没有取得过任何成绩。他们来美国巡演过几次，但那不是我们所熟知的1973年后那个由主音吉他手David Gilmour领导，发行了《 The Dark Side of the Moon》的Pink Floyd 。这是一个不同寻常的标志性迷幻乐团：他们早期的单曲《Arnold Layne》和《See Emily Play》分别在英国的榜单上排名第20和第6，而Pink Floyd的有趣之处就在于他们拒绝现场表演这些单曲。他们在现场总是混乱、即兴地表演，这使得很多来看演出的观众十分失望，因为乐队经常表演这些前卫的、即兴的东西长达15至20分钟，甚至是半个小时，而观众想要听到的是打榜单曲。相传一大群人就在楼座上把啤酒一类的东西泼向乐队，但乐队也没妥协，因为他们认为在录音室演唱单曲和现场表演是两回事，不应该混淆。《Interstellar Overdrive》就是一个很好的例子： 这首歌的调子一响起，他们便立马投入到了前卫的现场即兴表演中。这首歌来自他们1967年8月的专辑《Piper at the Gates of Dawn》。《Interstellar Overdrive》的有趣之处在于，它让我们看到那些在美国还没有被完全接受的东西是怎样进入伦敦的迷幻文化圈的。这首歌开头的乐句取自Arthur Lee领导的洛杉矶乐队Love，他们在1966年有一首有点平庸的打榜单曲叫《My Little Red Book》，这首歌最开始是主流流行乐界的明星Bert Backarack和Howell David写的。Pink Floyd的经纪人Peter Jenner听到了这首歌，他把开头的乐句哼给Syd Barrett听——Peter Jenner并没有这首歌的谱子， Syd Barrett也没有完全正确地记下它，因此Pink Floyd并没有很准确地复制旋律——该乐句就这么被用在了《Interstellar Overdrive》里。如果有机会的话，你应该去听听《My Little Red Book》，再和《Interstellar Overdrive》的开头比较一下，你会发现这两首歌的相似之处。这两句乐句的差异在很大程度上象征了美国西海岸和伦敦之间迷幻文化的差异。

让我们继续Pink Floyd的故事：1967年夏天，在他们录制《Piper at the Gates of Dawn》的那个录音室里，The Beatles正在录《Abbey Road》，Paul McCartney探出头来，听见了这支年轻乐队正在录制他们的第一张唱片。但是后来也许是因为迷幻剂，也许是因为精神上不稳定，或者两者都有，Syd开始出现精神不稳定的征兆——这不是什么好事情，他的行为开始反复无常。刚开始，他的朋友David Gilmour还进入乐队帮Syd处理一些事情。但终于有一天，他们决定演出不再带上Syd了，David Gilmour替代了Syd在乐队的重要地位。乐队继续前行，创作了很多伟大的唱片，这些唱片在英国都很成功。1968年的《A Saucerful of Secrets》和1970年的《Atom Heart Mother》是他们很重要的两张专辑，但彼时Pink Floyd一直没有在美国取得成功——直到1973年《The Dark Side of the Moon》发行，那真是一次巨大的成功，从许多方面看，没有任何一张专辑可以像它那样成功地把60年代末伦敦的迷幻美学带到了70年代。这也是Pink Floyd在70年代的一张概念专辑。提到概念专辑的历史，我们可以从The Beatles的《Sgt. Pepper》讲到Pink Floyd的《The Wall》。此外还有一些在地下文化中扮演重要角色的乐团：当Pink Floyd作为一支伦敦的地方性乐队时，从来没有取得过国际上的成功，但是有一些乐队做到了，例如Soft Machine，他们为迷幻乐带去了强烈的爵士乐影响。还有支叫Tomorrow的乐队，他们有几支打榜歌曲，最标志性的就是那首《My White Bicycle》。

有趣的是，后来去了Yes和Asia的Steve Howe当时在Tomorrow The Crazy World of Arthur Brown乐队有首代表作《Fire》，这首歌电台播放效果很好，70年代经常在美国电台播放。这个乐队里还有Emerson、Lake & Palmer里的Carl Palmer。我们所讲的60年代末伦敦迷幻文化的情况，还有一些在主流之外的地下乐队——这些事我们在美国肯定不会知道，除非你亲自到伦敦的看过他们的演出。在下篇文章中，我们将讲到一批在60年代末把迷幻元素真正加入英国音乐中的英国主流艺人。
body.en:
While San Francisco psychedelia was in full swing, London across the water developed a psychedelic culture with a subtle relationship to it.

Now let us cross the continent and the Atlantic—from San Francisco to London—to cover how psychedelic culture developed there, and some Anglo-American comparisons.

In the first phase before 1967, London shared some of San Francisco’s pattern: familiar mainstream bands held the charts, but later they also intertwined with London’s subculture. London’s psychedelic subculture was already there in 1965; as in San Francisco, in 1967 several psychedelic bands rose and the culture suddenly went national. Some of those bands succeeded in America; some did not. An interesting fact: people making psychedelic music in Britain actually knew little about San Francisco—flying in 1965–66 was not as common as now; not many people, especially 20- or 21-year-olds, went back and forth between San Francisco and New York. So Londoners’ information about San Francisco was hearsay or newspaper reports. Youth papers were few then, let alone TV—no internet or satellite TV; how would you know what was happening in San Francisco? Interestingly, on limited information these young people developed a psychedelic music that in some ways included San Francisco’s basic traits, but with a British accent—yet the two places had no direct link. Some people did travel between San Francisco and London, but few; among them was Beat poet Allen Ginsberg.

In fact San Francisco psychedelia and the Beats, with City Lights Bookstore and people like Lawrence Ferlinghetti, had already risen in the late 1950s—though the Beats chose jazz, not rock. Ginsberg not only mattered to Beat poetry’s rise; he also brought the idea that LSD heightens perception and fuels writing. In summer 1965 he came to London to help local poets organize readings and brought some San Francisco things with him. That summer they held “Poets of the World – Poets of Our Time” at the Royal Albert Hall; scholars often treat that gathering as, in a sense, the start of London’s underground psychedelic culture. People who had been to San Francisco shared what they had seen. In autumn 1965 Michael Hollingshead opened the World Psychedelic Center, which became a hub of London psychedelia. His work resembled Ken Kesey’s in San Francisco—another Johnny Appleseed of LSD and the counterculture. In a way this was what the underground was doing.

After the World Psychedelic Center opened, Indica Bookshop opened in February 1966 and mattered for spreading countercultural books. John Lennon went there and bought Timothy Leary’s The Psychedelic Experience—the Beatles’ 1966 “Tomorrow Never Knows” draws on it to some degree. In 1966 the London Free School was founded to offer free courses raising awareness of social and cultural topics and to circulate practical writing. Its paper International Times was a London Oracle or later Rolling Stone; that was October 1966. In December 1966 the UFO Club opened, with psychedelic night events.

Against London’s underground, an important mainstream moment was Time’s April 1966 story on “Swinging London”—if you came to London in 1966 you would see the Mod London Austin Powers spoofs: not very hippie, right? Carnaby Street fashion and Mod style were the mainstream then. While Time sold that London to Americans wanting a holiday, psychedelic culture was sprouting where tourists did not go. One of London psychedelia’s best bands was Pink Floyd, still in the early Syd Barrett lineup. Their first two singles mattered in Britain but did nothing in America. They toured the U.S. a few times—but that is not the post-1973 Pink Floyd led by David Gilmour that made The Dark Side of the Moon. This was a different landmark psychedelic band: early singles “Arnold Layne” and “See Emily Play” hit No. 20 and No. 6 in Britain. The interesting part: they refused to play those singles live. Shows were chaotic and improvisational, disappointing many who wanted chart hits while the band did avant-garde improvisation for 15–20 minutes or half an hour. Legend has crowds in the balcony pouring beer on them; the band did not yield—studio singles and live performance were different things. “Interstellar Overdrive” is a good example: once the riff starts they dive into avant-garde live improv. It is on August 1967’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn. Interestingly, it shows how things not fully accepted in America entered London psychedelia. The opening phrase comes from Arthur Lee’s L.A. band Love and their rather ordinary 1966 chart single “My Little Red Book,” first written by mainstream pop stars Burt Bacharach and Hal David. Pink Floyd’s manager Peter Jenner hummed the opening to Syd Barrett—Jenner had no sheet music, Barrett did not write it down perfectly, so they did not copy the melody exactly—and that phrase went into “Interstellar Overdrive.” If you can, hear “My Little Red Book” and compare the opening of “Interstellar Overdrive”; you will hear the likeness. The difference between those two phrases largely stands for differences between West Coast and London psychedelic culture.

Continue Pink Floyd’s story: in summer 1967, in the same studio where they cut Piper, the Beatles were recording at Abbey Road; Paul McCartney poked his head in and heard this young band making their first album. Later—perhaps psychedelics, mental instability, or both—Syd began to show signs of instability; his behavior grew erratic. At first friend David Gilmour joined to help Syd. Finally they decided not to take Syd onstage; Gilmour took his place. The band went on and made great records, successful in Britain. 1968’s A Saucerful of Secrets and 1970’s Atom Heart Mother are important, but Pink Floyd still had no U.S. success until 1973’s The Dark Side of the Moon—a huge hit that, in many ways, carried late-1960s London psychedelic aesthetics into the 1970s more successfully than any other album. It is also a 1970s Pink Floyd concept album. Concept-album history can run from the Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper to Pink Floyd’s The Wall. Other bands mattered underground: while Pink Floyd as a local London band had no international success yet, some did—Soft Machine brought strong jazz influence into psychedelia; Tomorrow had chart songs, most iconic “My White Bicycle.”

Interestingly, Steve Howe—later of Yes and Asia—was in Tomorrow. The Crazy World of Arthur Brown had the signature “Fire,” which radio played well and U.S. stations often aired in the 1970s. That band also included Carl Palmer of Emerson, Lake & Palmer. So: late-1960s London psychedelia, plus underground bands outside the mainstream—things Americans would not know unless they saw them live in London. Next: British mainstream artists who truly put psychedelic elements into British music at the end of the 1960s.
